physical_harm: Death caused to the deceased driver
number_of_offences: Number of offences/counts charged: 5; Number of offences finally upheld: 0
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the appellant's version of the incident, including his claim of self-defense against the deceased party who were pelting stones and shouting 'fire them', and found that the appellant had reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt.
witness_credibility: The court assessed that the prosecution's eye witnesses, PW-1, PW-2, PW-3, and PW-7, were declared hostile, and therefore, their evidence was not reliable to prove the incident as alleged by the prosecution.
post_offence_conduct: The appellant surrendered the gun recovered from the deceased party along with his own gun in the police station while registering the FIR and brought the deceased party's associates to the police station.

legal_representation.state: Balaji Srinivasan, AAG, B. Vinodh Kanna, Ms. S. Valarmathi, Ms. Pallavi Sengupta, M. Yogesh Kanna, Advs.

appeal_history.trial_court: Convicted under Sections 302, 203 IPC, Section 36-A and E of Tamil Nadu Forest Act, and Section 3 read with Section 25(1-B)(a) of the Arms Act
appeal_history.high_court: Partially allowed the appeal, altered conviction under Section 302 to Section 304 Part II IPC, acquitted from other charges
appeal_history.supreme_court: Allowed the appeal, set aside the impugned order, acquitted the appellant from all charges

prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant-A-1, while on duty, chased a lorry suspected of smuggling sandalwood, fired a gun shot which killed the driver, and then loaded sandalwood and a gun in the lorry. The appellant then falsely claimed he fired in self-defence. The prosecution sought conviction under Sections 302, 109, 203, 36-A and E of the Tamil Nadu Forest Act, and Sections 3 and 25(1-B)(a) of the Arms Act.
defence_argument: The appellant argued that he fired the gun shot in self-defence as the deceased party had started pelting stones at him and his driver, shouting 'fire them', thereby creating an immediate threat to his life and that of his driver. He was a forest ranger on duty and had a duty to protect forest produce and his own safety.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principles under Sections 96 to 106 of the IPC regarding the right of private defence, emphasizing that the right does not arise if there is time to seek public authorities' help, and that the person must have a reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt.
precedent_relied_upon: Amjad Khan v. Haji Mohammad Khan AIR 1952 SC 165; Darshan Singh v. State of Punjab & Anr. (2010) 2 SCC 333
